title: Elizabeth at Tilbury
text:
In the summer of 1588 the Spanish Armada sailed up the English Channel. Its plan was to escort a Spanish army from the Netherlands across to England. By early August the Armada had been driven past into the North Sea, but no one in England knew whether it would return, and an invasion from Flanders was still feared.

English troops were gathered at Tilbury, on the Thames east of London. Against the advice of those worried for her safety, Queen Elizabeth I went there and rode among the soldiers.

The text of her speech that has come down to us was recorded by Leonel Sharp, a chaplain who was present, in a letter published decades later. In it she says that she has been warned to beware of armed crowds for fear of treachery, but that she does not desire to live distrusting her faithful people. She has come, she says, resolved to live or die among them. Then the famous words: "I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too."

The invasion never came, and the speech became part of England's memory of the Armada.
lesson: Words carry weight when you stand where the danger is. Showing up in person tells people you share their risk.
source: Leonel Sharp's letter to the Duke of Buckingham, published in Cabala (1654)
caveat: The text survives only through Sharp's later version, so the exact wording is uncertain.
